content.text: Radioactive decay is random—we can't predict when a particular nucleus will decay. However, for large numbers of nuclei, we can predict how many will decay in a given time. Half-life is the key concept that allows us to make these predictions and has important applications from carbon dating to nuclear medicine.

Half-life is the time taken for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay, or equivalently, the time for the activity to halve. It is constant for a given isotope and unaffected by external conditions.
is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
Alternatively: the time for the activity (or count rate) to halve.
Not affected by temperature, pressure, or chemical state
Ranges from fractions of a second to billions of years

To find the half-life from a decay graph, pick any starting activity on the y-axis, find half that value, then read across to the curve and down to the time axis. The difference in time is the half-life. Repeat at different starting points and average for a more reliable result.
— After 2 half-lives, 1/4 remain. Decay continues indefinitely.
"Half-life is half the life of the sample"
— Half-life is the time for half to decay, not when the sample is gone.
"We can predict exactly when each nucleus decays"
— Decay is random. We can only predict probabilities.
— Nuclear properties are unaffected by physical conditions.
— Theoretically, some nuclei always remain. Practically, it becomes negligible.

Explain why radioactive decay is described as random and spontaneous.
After n half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)^n. So after 1 half-life: 1/2 remains; after 2: 1/4; after 3: 1/8; after 4: 1/16, and so on. A radioactive sample never fully decays to zero.

a) After 2 hours (1 half-life): 800 x 1/2 = 400 Bq. b) After 4 hours (2 half-lives): 800 x (1/2)^2 = 200 Bq. c) After 8 hours (4 half-lives): 800 x (1/2)^4 = 50 Bq.
— count the number of halvings and divide total time (calculation)
1/4 = (1/2)^2, so 2 half-lives have passed. Age = 2 x 5730 = 11,460 years.
1600 -> 800 -> 400 -> 200 -> 100 -> 50. Need 5 half-lives to drop below 100 Bq (to 50 Bq).
— 1600 x (1/2)^4 = 100 exactly, so need at least 5 (calculation)
The count rate halved (400 -> 200) in 15 minutes, so the half-life is 15 minutes.

Radioactive decay is random because it is impossible to predict when any individual nucleus will decay; each has a fixed probability per unit time. It is spontaneous because it occurs without any external trigger and is not affected by temperature, pressure, or chemical conditions.
— nuclear process governed by quantum probability (reasoning)
